========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, you know, I'm not really sure if "guilty" is the right word for it. I mean, I know I just said a few minutes ago that I feel ashamed and I get mad at myself, which I absolutely do, but... guilt? Guilt feels like something else entirely to me. 

Like, at my job, if I were to accidentally give a client the wrong quote on their auto insurance, or if I forgot to file a claim for them and it caused them a bunch of financial trouble, then I would definitely feel guilty, because I hurt somebody else, you know? I let them down and it affected their life. 

But with this... with the eating in the evenings... it's really just me. I'm just standing there in my own kitchen, usually by myself, looking at the empty cracker boxes and the dirty bowls left on the counter. I haven't hurt anyone else. So I don't really feel like I've committed a crime or done something wrong to another person that I need to feel guilty about. It's more just this... this intense, overwhelming frustration with my own lack of willpower. I'll be standing there, looking at the mess, thinking about how I was so incredibly good all day at the office, eating my little disciplined lunch while I made my calls, and then I just threw all that hard work away the second I walked through my own front door. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed feeling guilty, exactly. It's just... I'm just so annoyed that I have to go to the grocery store again to replace the things I ate, and I'm just tired of having that heavy, stretched-out feeling in my stomach. But guilt... no, I don't think I'd call it that. I'm just really, really mad at myself for not being able to just sit on the couch and watch TV like a normal person.

Once I get started on those nights, it's like I just keep going back to the kitchen, over and over again, even while I'm actively telling myself to stop. I'll still have my work shoes on, just pacing between the living room and the pantry, and my brain is saying, "You don't need this, you're not even hungry, just go sit down," but I just keep reaching for things. 

It's like I'm on autopilot and someone else programmed the destination. I really don't feel like I'm back in charge of myself until I hit that point where I'm just uncomfortably full. It’s like my stomach has to physically ache and stretch before the spell finally breaks and I'm me again, and I can finally just stop and walk away from the counter. But before 6 PM? Never happens. It's strictly an evening thing.

Oh, gosh, yes. Absolutely. The guilt is just... it's immense. It's like this heavy, wet blanket just drops right over me the very second that spell breaks and I realize what I've just done. I just get it in my head that I have to burn it all off, that I have to pay the penance for losing control. It's just this exhausting cycle of messing up and then punishing myself the whole next day to try and wipe the slate clean.

But then... then I get home after work, and it's like a switch just flips in my brain. \n\nI'll walk in the door, put my purse down, and I just start eating, and I end up eating way, way more than I ever intended to. It usually starts out okay, just making a normal dinner, but then... then I'll have a bowl of cereal. And then I'll open a box of crackers. And then I'm digging into whatever leftovers are sitting in the fridge, and then I absolutely have to have something sweet, so I'm finding cookies or whatever sweets I have around the kitchen... and this all happens so fast, just all within a couple of hours. I just keep going, and it's really starting to bother me because, like I said, I try so hard to be strict all day, and then the evening just completely falls apart on me.\n\nDoctor: How do you feel after these episodes of eating in the evenings?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's just this awful, defeated feeling, honestly. Because while it's happening, once I get started on those nights, it's like... it's like I'm not even the one driving anymore. I'll be standing there, maybe leaning against the counter where I put my keys and the mail down, and I'll actually be telling myself in my head, \"Okay, that's enough, you don't need any more, just go sit in the living room and turn on the TV.\" But it's like I can't even listen to my own voice. \n\nI just keep going back to the kitchen, opening the pantry, checking the fridge again, even while I'm practically begging myself to just stop and walk away. I end up looking at the empty cracker boxes or the dishes on the counter, and I just get so mad at myself. I think about how disciplined I was all day at the office, and then I just feel so ashamed that I couldn't stop myself until I was physically too full to keep going. It just ruins the whole rest of my night.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're eating much more quickly than usual during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Well, I'm not really sure if it's faster, exactly. I'll have the cereal, and then I'll find the crackers, and then I'm looking for the cookies. It's just one thing after another. I don't sit down and savor it or chat with anyone. It's just this steady, relentless grazing until I'm so full my stomach aches. So, yeah, I haven't really noticed if I'm eating quicker, just that I'm eating a lot more and I can't seem to make myself stop until I'm completely stuffed.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty after these episodes of eating in the evenings are over?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I'm not really sure if \"guilty\" is the right word for it. Guilt feels like something else entirely to me. \n\nLike, at my job, if I were to accidentally give a client the wrong quote on their auto insurance, or if I forgot to file a claim for them and it caused them a bunch of financial trouble, then I would definitely feel guilty, because I hurt somebody else, you know? Oh, absolutely. I mean, what other reason would there be, right? It's all about the math, really. It's like... well, it's like a bank account. Being in insurance, I look at everything as a matter of premiums and payouts, deficits and surpluses. When I have one of those nights where I just eat and eat, I'm basically overdrawing my account. Anyway, I just sit at my desk with my ice water, looking at policies, and I tell myself that the hunger is just me paying off the debt from the night before. 

But the food restriction isn't enough on its own to stop the weight gain, or at least I don't trust that it is. So I have to do the physical part, too. And at fifty, let me tell you, your knees really feel it when you're doing wind sprints or running bases like you're trying out for the Olympics. 

But I do it, even when I'm so tired I could just cry, because in my head, every drop of sweat is an ounce of weight I'm keeping off. If I didn't do all of that—if I just ate all that food and then went about a normal day—I'd blow up like a balloon. So, yes, the fasting, the extra-long hikes, pushing myself to the absolute limit at conditioning... it's 100% just to make sure I don't gain weight from what I did the night before.

Oh, without a doubt. I mean, my metabolism just isn't what it used to be. When you hit fifty, it’s like your body just decides to hold onto every single calorie, especially when you spend eight hours a day sitting at a desk writing insurance policies. If I just ate all that food and then woke up the next morning, had a normal breakfast, and went about my day without doing anything to counteract it? I'd probably put on five pounds in a week. It terrifies me, honestly. 

That fear is exactly why I do all of this. Like I was saying earlier—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it really is just how my life works right now—the next day after one of those nights, I'll tell myself I'm making up for it by skipping breakfast and lunch entirely. I just have to. And then I have to do the physical part to make absolutely sure the scale doesn't move. I'll go take an extra-long hike up the trail, or I'll be out there pushing harder at softball conditioning than anyone else on the team, even when I'm just bone-tired. 

And I mean, I really am exhausted. I'm running on empty because I haven't eaten all day, but I force myself to do it anyway. If I didn't push through that exhaustion and do the fasting and the extra exercise, all that food from the night before would just stick right to me. I'd have to buy a whole new work wardrobe, and I just bought these really nice tailored slacks from Macy's for a big client meeting next month, and they fit perfectly right now. I can't afford to let myself go and ruin that. So, yes, if I didn't restrict my food and work out like crazy the next day, I know for an absolute fact that I would gain weight, and I just can't let that happen.

Guilt feels like something else entirely to me. \n\nLike, at my job, if I were to accidentally give a client the wrong quote on their auto insurance, or if I forgot to file a claim for them and it caused them a bunch of financial trouble, then I would definitely feel guilty, because I hurt somebody else, you know? I'm just standing there in my own kitchen, usually by myself, looking at the empty cracker boxes and the dirty bowls left on the counter. I haven't hurt anyone else. It's more just this... this intense, overwhelming frustration with my own lack of willpower. Just what we've already talked about.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you were trying to get rid of the calories from one of these eating episodes in any way other than through exercise or restricting your food intake?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, I think we just went over this, didn't we? I don't have any secret methods or hidden tricks up my sleeve. \n\nI guess when you ask it like that, it makes me stop and think if maybe I do something subconsciously? I just wake up the next morning feeling this heavy, awful pit in my stomach, and I tell myself, \"Well, you really did it this time, so now you have to pay for it.\" And paying for it means not eating a single thing, just drinking my ice water, and then pushing myself on the trail or at softball practice until I feel like I'm going to collapse. That's the only way I know how to handle it. So, no, nothing else. It’s like my stomach has to physically ache and stretch before the spell finally breaks and I'm me again, and I can finally just stop and walk away from the counter. But before 6 PM? Never happens. It's strictly an evening thing.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've done something wrong after these eating episodes are over?\n\nPatient: Oh, gosh, yes. Absolutely. The guilt is just... it's immense. It's like this heavy, wet blanket just drops right over me the very second that spell breaks and I realize what I've just done. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, or maybe I've finally made it to the couch, and I just look at the empty boxes or the wrappers, and I just think, \"Why? Why did you do this again?\" It's this awful, sinking feeling of failure, really, because I know better. I'm a fifty-year-old woman, I manage complex insurance policies all day, I should be able to manage my own dinner, right? So, yes, I feel like I've done something terribly wrong. \n\nAnd because I feel so guilty, so ashamed of it, I always... well, I have this whole routine the next day to try and fix it. I'll tell myself I'm making up for it. So the next morning, I'll wake up and I'll just completely skip breakfast. Won't even look at the toaster. And then at the office—you know how I mentioned my sensible little salads or turkey wraps earlier? Well, after one of those bad nights, I won't even pack that. I'll just skip lunch entirely. I'll sit at my desk, and maybe my stomach is actually growling by 1 or 2 PM while I'm on the phone with a client, but I'll just drink ice water and ignore it, telling myself I don't need food after what I did the night before. \n\nAnd it doesn't even stop with the food, either. I feel like I have to physically work it off. So I'll force myself to take an extra-long hike. There's this trail system near my neighborhood, and usually I'd just do the short loop, but I'll make myself do the steep, two-hour trail, even if it's hot out and my legs feel like lead. Or... oh, I play in this women's slow-pitch softball league. It's usually a lot of fun, most of the ladies are around my age, but we do have these conditioning practices. If I had a bad episode the night before, I will push myself so much harder at softball conditioning. I'll run extra bases, I'll push through the drills, even when I am just completely, bone-deep tired and my body is begging me to stop. I just get it in my head that I have to burn it all off, that I have to pay the penance for losing control. It's just this exhausting cycle of messing up and then punishing myself the whole next day to try and wipe the slate clean.\n\nDoctor: Do you often restrict your food intake to very low calories or skip meals altogether on days following these episodes?\n\nPatient: Yes, exactly, that's... well, that's exactly what I was just getting at. It's almost like a strict rule I have for myself now. The very next day after one of those nights, I'll wake up and immediately tell myself that I'm making up for it. I won't even look at food. Skipping breakfast and lunch isn't just something that happens because I'm busy with clients or distracted at the office—it's very, very intentional. \n\nLike I was saying about sitting at my desk with just my ice water? I'll sit there, pulling up auto quotes or dealing with underwriting, and my stomach will be absolutely twisting in knots because it's empty, but I just refuse to eat. I tell myself, \"You had more than enough last night, you don't get to eat today.\" \n\nAnd then, on top of practically eating zero calories all day, I'll still force myself out onto that steep hiking trail, or I'll go to the softball field and just run myself ragged. I'll push so much harder at conditioning, doing those extra sprints between the bases even when my legs are shaking and I'm just completely, utterly tired. I just feel this intense need to balance the scales, you know? To erase the night before. It's exhausting, honestly, but I just can't seem to let myself off the hook.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these episodes of eating in the evenings?\n\nPatient: No, no, I don't do that. I know some people do, but that's just... I've never been able to bring myself to do that. The thought of it just makes me feel awful. I mean, my stomach will be hurting so much, just stretched tight like a drum, and I'll be sitting there on the couch, feeling so incredibly full and miserable, and maybe a part of me wishes I could just undo it right then and there. Even when I get the stomach flu—which, thankfully, isn't very often, maybe once every few years, usually if someone brings a bug into the office and we're all sharing the same coffee pot—I fight it as long as I can. I'll just lie there with a cool washcloth on my forehead, sipping ginger ale, doing everything in my power not to be sick. So the idea of doing it on purpose, night after night? No, that's not me at all. \n\nThat's why I rely so heavily on the skipping meals and the exercise the next day. Because since I can't—or won't—make myself sick to get rid of the food right away, I feel like I have to work twice as hard the next day to burn it off. That's why I'll push myself on that two-hour hike, or run those extra bases at softball practice until my lungs are burning. It's my way of purging it, I guess, just not... not the physical throwing up way. I just sweat it out and starve it out instead. But vomiting? No, never.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever use laxatives or diuretics to try and undo the effects of one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: No, no, I've never touched those either. I mean, I know what they are, of course. You see the commercials for them, or you walk down the pharmacy aisle at Walgreens when you're just trying to pick up some allergy medicine or maybe some cotton balls, and there they are. But I've never bought them. I've never even been tempted to, honestly. \n\nIt's sort of like the throwing up thing, I guess. Taking a pill to force my body to... well, to get rid of it that way... it just feels so unnatural and, honestly, a bit scary. I have this coworker, Brenda, she sits a few cubicles down from me, and she used to take these water pills—diuretics, I guess—because she said they helped her feel less bloated before big events. She took them before her daughter's wedding last spring. But she ended up feeling so dizzy and lightheaded at work one afternoon that we almost had to call someone. She was just sitting at her desk, white as a sheet, and I remember thinking, \"I am never putting myself in that position.\" I need to be sharp for my clients. No pills, no laxatives, nothing like that.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever engaged in any behaviors to try to compensate for the calories you consumed during these episodes, other than restricting your food intake and exercising?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't. I don't use anything else, no other tricks or anything. \n\nLike I said, I'm pretty structured. It's already like a full-time job on top of my actual full-time job, trying to manage the guilt and the calories and everything. So, no, nothing else. Just what we've already talked about.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you were trying to get rid of the calories from one of these eating episodes in any way other than through exercise or restricting your food intake?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, I think we just went over this, didn't we?
